transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Claire (Redwood Solutions), Maya (LinQware PM), Jon (LinQware Eng), Rachel (LinQware DS), Omar (LinQware Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Goal: Scope POC quality evaluation and load/benchmark plan.
- Focus areas: golden prompts, regression suite, hallucination/format checks, scoring and pass/fail gates, bech/bench (sic) load sizing, security requirements for Private/Dedicated.
- Outcome: Agree on dataset sizes, scoring approach, timelines, and next steps to run baseline and end-to-end bench.

Topics: golden prompt set; regression playlist; hallucination detection; telemetry/metrics; throughput/latency targets; SSO/KMS; rollout criteria

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) ---
00:00 Alex (Redwood): Okay good morning, everyone, uh this is Alex from Redwood, thanks for joining. We wanted to run through the POC quality plan for LinQware's KnowledgeAssist pilot, so we'll cover golden prompts, regression tests, format checks and the bench spec.
00:14 Maya (LinQware): Thanks Alex, and hi all. Quick context: our main thing is to reduce hallucination in policy answers and keep the response format strict for downstream parsing. We're aiming to ship a beta in Q4 so POC needs to be quick.
00:28 Samir (Redwood SE): Sweet. Quick qual check — what's your current stack? Are you running in GCP, any VPC needs?
00:34 Jon (LinQware): We're on GCP, VPC with private subnets. We'll probably need a VPC peering or private link for dedicated. Also we use Cloud KMS for keys.
00:44 Omar (LinQware Sec): And SOC2 is in process; SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs are must-haves. We will need to see HSM/KMS integration details.
00:55 Claire (Redwood): Noted — we can share the security pack. We'll include our KMS integration patterns, audit log retention options and sample SAML config.
01:05 Rachel (LinQware DS): On metrics, we're focused on precision for entities, hallucination rate, structural correctness (JSON schema adherence) and latency P95/P99. We also want a simple human-review sampling plan.
01:20 Samir (Redwood SE): Makes sense. For the quality plan itself, we typically recommend: a golden set (authoritative prompts + expected outputs), a larger regression set (2–5k examples ideally), automated checks (schema validation, hallucination heuristics), and an embedding-similarity / metric-based scoring with human thresholds.
01:38 Maya: For golden set size — what do you normally see? 200? 500?
01:44 Alex: For a POC 150–300 strong golden prompts is common. Enough to cover core intents and edge cases. We had good signal with 200 in similar pilots. For regression we usually aim for 1–3k depending on diversity; 2k is a good tradeoff.
01:58 Jon: Ok that sounds realistic. What about scoring — is it purely BLEU or something else?
02:05 Samir: We avoid relying on BLEU alone. For knowledge-grounded answers we pair two things: (1) embedding similarity between output and reference for semantic match, and (2) token-level schema/format checks and hallucination heuristics — e.g., external-entity mentions that don't map to the source, overly confident assertions. We also surface LM log-prob features if accessible.
02:25 Rachel: How do you detect hallucination automatically?
02:29 Samir: A mix: source overlap metrics (does the answer cite or overlap with the canonical doc), entity cross-checks against a golden KB, and embedding-distance thresholds. We also run a small LM-based hallucination classifier sometimes — not perfect but helps triage.
02:43 Alex: We will provide a sample hallucination rule-set and a small Python harness for running these checks.
02:50 Claire: Also we recommend a mixing of pass/fail gates and soft scoring. For example: if schema fails — immediate fail. If hallucination above threshold — fail. Otherwise use weighted score across relevance, factuality and format where >85% passes.
03:06 Maya: Good. Latency targets — our product needs sub-300ms median and P95 under 600ms for short outputs. Is that reasonable?
03:14 Samir: For hosted small-to-medium models, median under 200–300ms is achievable for short prompts; P95 depends on batching and KV cache warmness. If you want strict P99 < 500ms, that often implies dedicated capacity and more tuning.
03:30 Jon: For load, our beta expects ~200 RPS peak across users, with spikes to 350 for short windows. What sizing do you recommend?
03:38 Alex: For 200 RPS we suggest a dedicated pool for baseline with autoscale for spikes. For benchmarking during POC, we'll run synthetic traffic with ramp to 400 RPS to validate burst behavior. We will share our load script.
03:52 Rachel: When you say synthetic traffic — will you use real KV cache patterns? Our real usage has high prefix reuse so the effective token cost is lower.
04:01 Samir: Good point — we can instrument a replay using anonymized real traces if you can share session sketches. If not, we'll simulate a mix of high-prefix reuse and cold-requests. That helps understand cache hit benefits.
04:16 Omar: Security constraints — we require that logs with PII are redacted and that data residency stays in our region. Also IP allowlisting and SSO enforced.
04:27 Claire: We can set up a Private deployment with customer-managed network; audit logs can be configured and token-level redaction is supported with policies. We'll send the config doc.
04:40 Maya: Timeline — what does a 4-week POC look like?}
04:44 Alex (Redwood): Typical cadence we propose: Week 0 (this week): finalize golden set and regression plan. Week 1: baseline runs and initial quality scoring. Week 2: iteration on prompts and config, run load tests. Week 3: final regression & quality report + recommendations and decision gate. That maps to three full weeks of runs but we can compress some tasks.
05:03 Jon: If we compress, what's the minimum to get meaningful signal?
05:07 Samir: At minimum: 200 golden prompts + 1k regression + a 24–48 hour baseline run to collect latency and quality — gives directional signal. For deeper perf numbers, need the full load tests.
05:20 Rachel: Scoring rubric specifics — can you spell out the weights?
05:25 Samir: Proposed: 40% factual consistency (embedding match + KB checks), 30% format/schema adherence, 20% relevance/intent match, 10% latency penalty (if P95 > target reduce score). Human review samples for borderline cases.
05:40 Maya: That seems fair. How do we handle multi-intent prompts and normalization of outputs? Our outputs must be strict JSON with a 'source' array and 'answer' string.
05:50 Samir: We'll run a JSON schema validator as first-class check. If schema fails it's a hard fail. For multi-intent, golden prompts should include examples that show how to format multi-intent outputs. We'll ask for canonical expected outputs in the golden set.
06:06 Alex: A few implementation notes: we will provide a sample test harness repo — Python-based — that runs the golden set, computes embedding similarity (using our reference model), validates schema, runs hallucination heuristics, and emits a per-example report. We will also add a load-driver to simulate RPS and measure hardware counters.
06:26 Jon: For embedded similarity, can we use our choice of model or must we use Redwood's embedding endpoint?
06:31 Claire: You can run your own embedder but to keep scoring consistent use the same embedder for both reference and candidate. We'll document recommended models and cosine thresholds. If you run embeddings outside Redwood, share the vectors for reproducibility.
06:44 Rachel: For thresholds, what numbers are typical?
06:47 Samir: For semantic match often >0.78 cosine for short answers, but it varies. We'll recommend tuning on a holdout. For hallucination heuristics a simple rule is: if mention of external entity with no source overlap and embedding distance >0.25 from any doc segment, flag. Again, approximate.
07:06 Maya: About human review — what's the sampling rate usable?
07:10 Alex: For POC, 5–10% random sampling plus all failed/flagged examples is typical. Human review rubric we can share.
07:19 Jon: Can Redwood host the regression runs or do we need to run internally? Concerns about sending data out.
07:24 Claire: Two options: Hosted Redwood API under contract with data retention policy, or Private/Dedicated where runtime is in your VPC. For early POC we can run in hosted with redaction; for full validation we recommend Dedicated/Private.
07:39 Omar: We'll prefer Private for final runs. For the POC can we do hosted but with redaction and NDA?
07:44 Alex: Yes, that's common — hosted pilot with strict masking then final bench on Private.
07:49 Maya: Any templates for the golden prompt CSV? What columns do you expect?
07:52 Samir: Template: id, prompt_text, expected_output, intent_tag, notes, related_doc_ids, level_of_strictness (hard/soft). We'll attach CSV example.
08:06 Maya: Good. Let's talk about the benchmark spec: what metrics exactly will you provide?
08:10 Alex: We'll produce a benchmark report with: throughput (RPS), median/P95/P99 latency, token cost estimate, success rate on golden set, hallucination rate, schema failure rate, average scoring breakdown, and resource utilization.
08:25 Jon: Do you provide cost modeling for token and infra?
08:28 Claire: Yes, we'll include per-query token cost estimates and a projected monthly cost for your expected workload under various quantization configs.
08:36 Rachel: For the regression suite, we want nightly runs. Is Redwood able to run scheduled regressions against pinned model versions?
08:43 Samir: Yes, we support pinned model versions and scheduled regression runs. We'll show how to pin, roll back and set automatic alerts on regressions.
08:55 Maya: What's the acceptance criteria to move to production?
08:58 Alex: Suggested gate: Golden set pass rate >= 90% (weighted as earlier), hallucination rate < 2% on sampled production traffic, latency P95 under 600ms, and security checklist completed (SAML + KMS + audit logs). If those met, proceed to Dedicated rollout.
09:16 Omar: For audit logs, retention needs are 12 months and log export to our SIEM — can you support that?
09:22 Claire: Yes, export options are supported; we'll include the SIEM integration guide.
09:29 Maya: Ok timeline recap — can we get an email with the checklist and the CSV template by Monday?
09:33 Alex: Yes, we'll send the package Monday along with the load script.
09:38 Jon: For the load test on week of 2026-09-27, do you need anything from our side now?
09:42 Samir: We'll need anonymized trace samples (session prefixes), a test account for the environment, and the golden prompts. Also a list of expected peak RPS windows.
09:53 Maya: Noted. We'll aim to deliver golden prompts and traces by 9/17.
09:58 Alex: Great. Quick Q&A before we wrap?
10:02 Rachel: How do you handle model rollbacks if a regression appears post-rollout?
10:06 Samir: We support instant rollbacks to pinned versions, and automatic fallback policies to a more conservative variant if anomaly detectors fire.
10:14 Maya: Any blockers on our side you anticipate?
10:16 Claire: Mostly data sharing (golden prompts, traces) and confirming security controls. If you can sign the addendum for hosted pilot data handling that'll speed things.
10:26 Omar: We'll review the addendum.
10:29 Alex: Okay, let's recap next steps in chat: we'll share the security pack, CSV template, benchmark harness link, and schedule the load test for week of 9/27. Action items in the notes. Thanks everyone.
10:42 Maya: Thanks all.
10:46 (call ends)
